testicular-cancer.name: Testicular cancer
aliases: germ cell tumour of the testis
testicular-cancer.definition: Testicular cancer is a cancer that starts in a testicle, one of the two glands in the scrotum.
testicular-cancer.overview: Testicular cancer often causes no symptoms, and when it does the most common sign is a lump or swelling in a testicle. It can affect anyone with testicles, including trans women and non-binary people, and Macmillan says it is most likely between the ages of 25 and 40. Most lumps in the scrotum have other causes, and testicular cancer is rare. It is generally very treatable, and removing the affected testicle is the main treatment when the cancer has not spread.
causes: Cancer Research UK says doctors do not know what causes most cases
Cancer cells grow from germ cells, the cells that make sperm, in one of the two main types, seminoma and non-seminoma
riskFactors: Abnormal cells found in a testicle
A family history of testicular cancer
signs: A lump or swelling in a testicle, or a testicle that has become larger
A scrotum that feels heavy, firm or hard
complications: Spread to the lungs, abdomen, pelvis, back or brain
Effects on fertility from chemotherapy, radiotherapy or surgery to the lymph nodes at the back of the abdomen
Lower testicular hormone function after treatment, needing follow-up
testicular-cancer.diagnosis: A GP asks about symptoms and general health, then checks the testicles and the lymph nodes. If cancer is possible there may be an urgent referral to hospital, which does not definitely mean cancer. An ultrasound scan of the scrotum is the quickest and most accurate test, and blood tests for substances called tumour markers are also used. A tissue examination that confirms the diagnosis needs the affected testicle to be removed.
testicular-cancer.treatment: The NHS says treatment includes surgery, radiotherapy and chemotherapy, depending on the type of tumour and whether it has spread. MedlinePlus says removing the testicle (orchiectomy) is the main treatment for cancer that has not spread, and that chemotherapy is also used. Sperm banking can be offered before treatment other than removal of the testicle.
testicular-cancer.prevention: No sure way to prevent testicular cancer is described by the sources, because the cause is not known in most cases. NHS pages encourage getting to know how the testicles normally feel so that a change can be noticed and checked.
testicular-cancer.seekCare: The NHS advises seeing a GP about a lump or swelling in one or both testicles, or a testicle that is getting bigger. A routine GP appointment is the usual route, and one NHS trust says a local sexual health clinic can also examine the testicles. Most lumps turn out to have other causes, but changes are worth having checked.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of testicular cancer?
sections.body:
MedlinePlus says testicular cancer often causes no symptoms at all. The NHS lists a lump or swelling in a testicle, a testicle getting bigger, an ache or pain in a testicle or the scrotum, and a scrotum that feels heavy, firm or hard. A lump may be small and firm, and one NHS trust describes it as possibly the size of a pea or larger.

Less common symptoms listed by the NHS include an ache in the back or lower tummy, losing weight without trying, a cough, and a sore or swollen chest. MedlinePlus adds that enlarged breast tissue can be a sign, although it can occur normally in teenage boys. When the cancer has spread, MedlinePlus says symptoms can appear in the lungs, abdomen, pelvis, back or brain.

Lumps in the scrotum have many different causes, and one NHS trust notes that testicular cancer is rare.

sections.heading: What causes testicular cancer and who is more likely to get it?
sections.body:
Cancer Research UK says doctors do not know what causes most cases of testicular cancer. It lists an undescended testicle, abnormal cells in a testicle and a family history among the things that may raise the risk. A published editorial also lists a previous testicular cancer, infertility, age and ethnicity as factors. Having a risk factor does not mean a person will develop the disease.

Macmillan says testicular cancer is most likely to happen between the ages of 25 and 40. One UK hospital says non-seminomas usually affect younger people aged 15 to 35, and seminomas people aged 25 to 55.

The two main types, seminoma and non-seminoma, are both germ cell tumours, and a mix of the two can occur.

sections.heading: Checking the testicles and seeing a GP
sections.body:
The NHS advises seeing a GP about a lump or swelling in one or both testicles, or if a testicle is getting bigger. An NHS trust suggests getting to know how the testicles normally feel, with a check about once a month, so that a new lump is noticed. Macmillan says it is still important to have any change checked.

Checking the testicles can feel awkward for anyone. Macmillan notes that a trans woman may feel uncomfortable or upset about checking this part of the body, but that changes should still be checked. One NHS trust says a local sexual health clinic can examine the testicles for anyone who prefers not to see a GP.

The GP asks about symptoms and general health, then checks the testicles and the lymph nodes. If cancer is possible, an urgent referral to hospital may follow, and the NHS stresses that this does not definitely mean cancer.

sections.heading: How is testicular cancer diagnosed?
sections.body:
Macmillan says an ultrasound scan is the quickest and most accurate test. An NHS trust describes hospital tests that usually include a scrotal ultrasound and blood tests for tumour markers called AFP and HCG. A sample of tissue can confirm the diagnosis, but it needs the affected testicle to be removed.

The two main types of testicular cancer, seminoma and non-seminoma, are treated differently, so identifying the type is part of the diagnosis. The treatment plan also depends on whether the cancer has spread.

Further scans may be used to see whether the cancer has spread, and the results guide the choice of treatment.

sections.heading: How is testicular cancer treated?
sections.body:
The NHS lists surgery, radiotherapy and chemotherapy as treatments, depending on the type of tumour and whether it has spread. MedlinePlus says removal of the testicle, called orchiectomy, is the main treatment for cancer that has not spread. Having one testicle removed does not usually affect fertility, according to an NHS guide.

Chemotherapy is also used, and MedlinePlus says it has greatly improved survival for both seminomas and non-seminomas. Seminomas may sometimes need radiotherapy after surgery to help stop the cancer coming back. For an early non-seminoma, close follow-up called surveillance or a short course of chemotherapy may be recommended.

The specialist team explains which options fit the type and stage of the cancer.

sections.heading: Fertility, follow-up and living with testicular cancer
sections.body:
Chemotherapy, radiotherapy and surgery to the lymph nodes at the back of the abdomen can each affect fertility. Because of this, sperm banking can be offered before any treatment other than removal of the testicle. Banking has limits, as a low sperm count, poor sperm quality and the freezing process can all affect the sperm.

Some people already have a low sperm count at diagnosis, so they may be told that no sperm can be banked. Orchid and Macmillan both provide information on fertility and sex after testicular cancer.

After treatment, testicular function can decline, so follow-up includes watching for signs of low hormone levels. Testicular cancer is generally described as highly treatable, and MedlinePlus calls it one of the most curable cancers.

faqs.q: Is a lump in a testicle always cancer?
faqs.a: No. Lumps in the scrotum have many different causes, and one NHS trust notes that testicular cancer is rare. The NHS still advises seeing a GP about a lump or swelling in one or both testicles, or a testicle that is getting bigger. A referral to hospital for tests does not definitely mean cancer.

MedlinePlus describes testicular cancer as one of the most treatable and curable cancers. The NHS says treatment depends on the type of tumour and whether it has spread. A specialist team can explain what to expect in an individual case.

faqs.q: Does removing a testicle affect fertility?
faqs.a: An NHS guide says having one testicle removed does not usually affect fertility. Chemotherapy and radiotherapy can affect fertility, so sperm banking can be offered before those treatments. Orchid has a page on fertility and testicular cancer.

faqs.q: Can trans women and non-binary people get testicular cancer?
faqs.a: Yes. Testicular cancer can affect anyone who has testicles, including trans women and non-binary people assigned male at birth. Macmillan notes that checking this part of the body may feel uncomfortable or upsetting for a trans woman, and that changes should still be checked.

faqs.q: Does testicular cancer always cause symptoms?
faqs.a: No. MedlinePlus says testicular cancer often causes no symptoms at all. When symptoms do appear, the NHS lists a lump or swelling, a larger testicle, an ache or pain, and a heavy, firm or hard scrotum.
